prompt:

(ticker BSBR), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "BSBR", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},

Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?

   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?

   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Banco Santander (Brasil) S.A.
markets: Retail banking and current accounts in Brazil
Consumer credit, credit cards and payroll loans
Wholesale and investment banking (Santander Corporate & Investment Banking Brazil)
Insurance, investments and asset management distribution

mission.statement: To help people and businesses prosper
mission.source: Banco Santander Group purpose (santander.com, 'Our culture'); Santander Brasil states it in Portuguese on santander.com.br as contributing to the prosperity of people and businesses
mission.plain: The bank says it exists to help Brazilians and Brazilian companies do better with their money.

about.plain: Santander Brasil is one of Brazil's biggest banks and is about 90% owned by Spain's Banco Santander. People keep their money there, use its cards and app, and borrow to buy cars, homes or to run a business. It earns most of its money from the interest it charges on loans, plus fees for cards, accounts and services. It also helps big companies raise money and trade currencies.
about.customers: About 76 million Brazilian people and businesses, 34 million of them active, from ordinary savers to large corporations.
about.everyday: The red Santander logo is on hundreds of bank branches and thousands of cash machines across Brazil, and on millions of credit cards.

money.part: Banking for people and smaller businesses
money.plain: loans, cards, accounts, car finance and insurance
corporate loans, markets and investment banking

result.summary: Santander Brasil has a real but modest advantage: scale, a large deposit base and the backing of a global parent give it cheap funding and a brand millions of Brazilians know. It is clearly the number three private bank behind Itaú and Bradesco, though, earns lower returns than Itaú (recurring ROAE was 12.5% in 2Q26), and faces fast-growing digital rivals such as Nubank that have taken customers with low-fee products.

pricingPower.evidence: IFRS fee and commission income rose 7.8% to R$25,522M in 2025, but net interest income grew only 1.7% to R$57,634M while credit impairments reached R$29,540M, and in 2Q26 NII fell 0.4% year on year with recurring ROAE dropping to 12.5%. Its loan spreads are set by Selic rates and competition from Itaú, Bradesco and Nubank, not by Santander.

moats.evidence: The Santander name is well known in Brazil (76.2 million customers in June 2026), but brand alone does not let it charge more than Itaú or Bradesco.
Salary accounts, payroll loans and bundled cards make customers somewhat sticky, but Pix instant payments and open finance have made switching between Brazilian banks much easier.
Banking has few network effects; Pix made payments interoperable across all banks, so Santander's network gives little advantage.
With R$1.29 trillion of assets and R$621bn of customer deposits at June 30, 2026, it has funding and technology scale (efficiency ratio 39.3% in 2Q26), though Itaú is larger and more profitable.
Brazilian banking is concentrated among a handful of large banks, which limits new full-service entrants, though digital banks have still won millions of customers.
It is an incumbent branch bank being counter-positioned by digital lenders such as Nubank and Inter, not the other way round.
It has credit-scoring and risk know-how in segments such as vehicle finance and payroll loans, but these processes are not clearly better than peers'.
Access to the global Santander group's technology platforms and capital is a resource local rivals lack, but it is not exclusive in a way that blocks competition.

customers.evidence: Customers rose 6% to 76.2 million and active customers 3% to 34.4 million (June 2026), but in the Central Bank's Q1 2026 complaints ranking Santander was 6th worst with 34.49 valid complaints per million clients, versus 10.65 for Nubank and 19.36 for Banco do Brasil.

talent.evidence: Santander Brasil ranked 20th in LinkedIn Top Companies Brazil 2026 (Itaú was 1st, Nubank 11th); it had 47,327 employees in June 2026 and changed CEO in July 2026.

product.evidence: It offers a full range of banking, card, auto-finance and investment products, but no independent benchmark shows it as best in class, and digital banks rank far better on complaints.

competitors.name: Itaú Unibanco

marketShare.market: Fee and commission income of Brazil's three largest private banks (Itaú, Bradesco, Santander Brasil)
marketShare.measure: share of combined IFRS fee and commission income, calculated from each bank's FY2025 Form 20-F (Itaú: commissions and banking fees)

marketShare.market: Net profit of Brazil's three largest private banks
marketShare.measure: share of combined IFRS profit attributable to the parent, calculated from each bank's FY2025 Form 20-F

threats: Digital banks (Nubank, Inter, C6, Mercado Pago) taking card, account and personal-loan customers with lower fees
Pix and open finance lowering switching costs and payment fees
High Selic rates and household indebtedness pushing up credit losses (cost of risk 3.81% and 90-day NPL ratio 3.3% in 2Q26, up from 2.6% a year earlier)
Itaú's superior returns and scale in the most profitable segments
Labour lawsuits and provisions (a non-recurring R$291M labour provision in 2Q26)
Brazilian real volatility and tax changes on interest on capital
Strategy and governance uncertainty from the July 2026 CEO change and the parent's exchange offer for minority shares, which could lead to NYSE delisting

ceo.name: Gilson Finkelsztain
ceo.background: Production engineer from PUC-Rio with INSEAD executive training; career at Citibank, J.P. Morgan and Santander (2011-2013), CEO of Cetip from 2013 and of exchange operator B3 from 2017 to 2026; became Santander Brasil CEO on July 1, 2026, succeeding Mario Leão.

c1.evidence: Brazilian banking is a mature industry, and Santander Brasil is the third-largest private bank behind Itaú and Bradesco, not the leader of an emerging one.

c2.evidence: Customers choose it for its branch and ATM network (858 stores and 5,693 ATMs in June 2026), full product range and global parent, but these advantages are shared by Itaú and Bradesco and are being eroded by digital banks.

c3.evidence: Most Brazilians recognise Santander, but it is not the default leader (Itaú is), and its Q1 2026 Central Bank complaints index of 34.49 per million clients suggests customers are not strong promoters.

c4.evidence: It repeats the group purpose of helping people and businesses prosper, but management communication centres on ROE recovery, a goal of about 20% by 2028, rather than a distinctive mission.

c6.evidence: “big bank, red, Spanish, fees”: the name is familiar and seen as solid, but the impression is mixed, as complaints about fees and service are common.

c7.evidence: Brazil's credit market is large and still underpenetrated, and Santander's expanded loan portfolio grew 5.8% to R$714.8bn in the year to June 2026, but this is steady growth rather than a secular boom.

c8.evidence: It can grow in agribusiness, wealth management, insurance and digital products (it merged the Esfera loyalty program into the bank in 2026), but its market is essentially Brazil.

m1.evidence: Gilson Finkelsztain only became CEO on July 1, 2026, and has not yet set out a long-term vision for the bank; at B3 he diversified the exchange into data and technology.

m2.evidence: He is a hired professional manager at a subsidiary 89.7% owned by Banco Santander S.A., not a founder.

m4.evidence: There is not yet enough record from his first months at Santander Brasil to judge his leadership style there.

m5.evidence: It is too early to judge his culture-building at Santander Brasil, which follows the group's 'Simple, Personal and Fair' culture.

m6.evidence: He trained as a production engineer and pushed technology and data at B3 (buying Neoway and Neurotech), but his career has been in treasury, markets and management.

m7.evidence: No public evidence either way about his character beyond a long record as a respected market-infrastructure executive.

m7b.evidence: No record found of a commencement speech by Gilson Finkelsztain at a top university.

m8b.evidence: He is known as a low-profile, technocratic executive rather than a distinctive public personality.

m9.evidence: At B3 (2017-2026) he led the Cetip-BM&FBovespa integration, and revenue more than doubled with R$40.1bn returned to shareholders, but he has no record yet at Santander Brasil, whose recurring ROAE fell to 12.5% in 2Q26.

m10.evidence: The bank runs a fairly efficient cost base (efficiency ratio 39.3% in 2Q26), but it is not known for a culture of frugality.

c10.evidence: It gives 76 million Brazilians access to accounts, credit and payments, which matters, but its impact is limited to Brazil and is easily replaced by other banks.

p2.evidence: Running a R$1.29 trillion regulated bank is hard and important to Brazil's economy, but the products themselves are standard banking.

f1.evidence: IFRS total income rose from R$48,242M in 2020 to R$74,997M in 2025, but it dipped in 2023 (R$65,864M vs R$66,475M in 2022).

f2.evidence: Pre-tax profit fell from 38.7% of total income in 2021 to 22.3% in 2025, as credit impairments rose from R$17.1bn to R$29.5bn.

f3.evidence: As a bank it is highly leveraged (total liabilities of R$1,161bn against equity of R$129bn in June 2026), though equity is positive and the CET1 ratio was 11.2%.

f4.evidence: Operating income before tax was R$24,750M in 2021 but only R$16,729M in 2025, and bank operating cash flow swings with deposits and loans.

v1.evidence: Nothing makes its accounts or loans clearly better than Itaú's, Bradesco's or Nubank's for an ordinary customer.

v2.evidence: It was 20th in LinkedIn Top Companies Brazil 2026, behind Itaú (1st), Banco do Brasil (6th) and Nubank (11th).

c5.evidence: Its customers and borrowers would notice if it disappeared, but Itaú, Bradesco, Banco do Brasil and digital banks could absorb them, so few would truly miss it.
